prompt: The city wants better flow and safe crossings. Which question fits the first fixed-phase queue prototype?

options.text: Which crossing time is suitable for all pedestrians?
options.feedback: The prototype has vehicle arrivals and signal phases. Answering a crossing-time question requires information about pedestrians, geometry and timing.

options.text: Which detector should the city purchase?
options.feedback: Choosing hardware requires sensing and interface needs that the first queue experiment leaves open.

options.text: Can different arrival patterns leave different queues under the same phases?
options.feedback: Arrivals, phases and queues are part of the prototype. Varying arrivals while holding the phases fixed isolates a question it can answer.

prompt: Two groups agree to improve the intersection but give different meanings to “better.” What is the next useful step?

options.text: Identify each group’s intended outcome and choose one uncertainty to investigate.
options.feedback: A driver’s queue and a pedestrian’s crossing opportunity call for different observations. Naming both helps turn a shared intent into meaningful criteria.

options.text: Make the shortest vehicle queue the acceptance criterion for everyone.
options.feedback: Queue length describes one outcome for one group. It leaves the crossing concern unanswered.

options.text: Choose adaptive control so that everyone can work to one design.
options.feedback: Selecting a controller settles the proposed mechanism before the team has agreed which outcomes it should improve.
